name: Sulforaphane

lead: Sulforaphane is an isothiocyanate that forms when the enzyme myrosinase converts glucoraphanin in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and kale after chopping or chewing. Broccoli sprouts are the richest common source.

People interested in skin and healthy aging take it in broccoli sprouts or supplement form, linking it to its role in cell-protective pathways. Human trials have looked at autism, glucose control, schizophrenia and cancer prevention rather than appearance outcomes.

paras: It is eaten as raw or lightly prepared broccoli and sprouts, or taken as broccoli sprout extract capsules. Cooking can change how much sulforaphane forms.
Trials report mild gastrointestinal effects. It is a food compound and supplement; people with medical conditions or taking medication usually consult a clinician.

Extract of broccoli sprouts protects from ultraviolet radiation

Proposed cell-protective effects relevant to skin and aging
angle.text: Sulforaphane is taken through crucifers or extracts with the idea of supporting skin and healthy aging. Human trials to date examine metabolic and neurological outcomes.

lead: Sulforaphane is a phytochemical in the isothiocyanate group, stored in cruciferous vegetables as its precursor glucoraphanin and formed when the enzyme myrosinase acts after the plant is chopped or chewed. Broccoli sprouts contain the most glucoraphanin among common sources, and broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, cauliflower, bok choy, kale and watercress also supply it.[1][2][3]

People interested in skin and healthy ageing eat broccoli and sprouts or take sprout-extract supplements. The appearance chain proponents describe runs from sulforaphane, to activation of the cell's own protective enzymes, to less UV-related redness and oxidative stress in skin, to a healthier-looking complexion over time. The strongest human skin finding is a 2007 Johns Hopkins study in which a topical extract of sprouts lessened UV-induced redness in six volunteers.[4][5] In physique communities the compound is also mentioned in discussions of hormone balance and recovery, based largely on forum claims.[6][7][8]

Human oral-supplement trials have examined glucose control, autism, ADHD, schizophrenia and lung-cancer prevention rather than skin appearance.[9][10][11][12][13] Wikipedia states there is no substantial clinical research showing a cancer benefit from dietary sulforaphane, while the Linus Pauling Institute describes limited human data and no serious adverse effects reported in people.[1][3]
infobox: Broccoli sprouts; also broccoli, kale, cabbage, cauliflower[1]
Food, sprout extract capsules, topical extract in research[3][4]
Topical UV-redness study (2007); prediabetes trial (2025); autism trial (2021)[9][10][4]

paras: Sulforaphane has the preferred IUPAC name 1-isothiocyanato-4-(methanesulfinyl)butane and the formula C6H11NOS2. It has two possible stereoisomers because of a stereogenic sulfur atom.[1] It occurs in cruciferous vegetables as glucoraphanin, a glucosinolate, which the enzyme myrosinase converts into sulforaphane when plant tissue is damaged by chopping or chewing.[1][2] The review in the Journal of Medicinal Food describes it as metabolised through the mercapturic acid pathway after conjugation with glutathione.[2]

The Linus Pauling Institute notes that glucosinolate levels vary with species, growing and storage conditions and processing, and that in one survey raw mustard greens yielded the most isothiocyanates and raw cauliflower the least.[3] Grokipedia says glucoraphanin in young broccoli sprouts can be 10 to 100 times higher than in mature heads.[14]

Chopping raw vegetables releases myrosinase, and cooking inactivates it; the Linus Pauling Institute says light steaming for under five minutes preserves some enzyme activity, and that when myrosinase is inactive, gut bacteria usually begin the breakdown, making their conversion the limiting step.[3] Wikipedia says that when broccoli is cooked, sulforaphane converts into a thiourea derivative and some 1,2,4-trithiolane.[1] Forum posts about cooked broccoli, olive oil and garlic reflect interest in preparation, though the claims there are anecdotal.[15][16]

A comparison in the Linus Pauling Institute summary reports that broccoli supplements lacking myrosinase delivered far less isothiocyanate than fresh sprouts, with peak plasma metabolite levels about eight times higher after fresh sprouts and urinary levels about five times higher. It also notes that some products are standardised to glucosinolate or sulforaphane content and that sprouts certified to contain at least 73 mg of glucoraphanin per ounce are sold in some stores.[3]

Grokipedia states that sulforaphane was first isolated and structurally characterised in 1992 from broccoli by Paul Talalay and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University.[14] Talalay, a pharmacology professor, later led the 2007 skin study.[4][5] Wikipedia lists sulforaphane among histone deacetylase inhibitors and among experimental cancer-drug candidates in laboratory research.[1]

Researchers describe sulforaphane as activating the Nrf2 pathway, which increases expression of antioxidant and detoxification enzymes such as NQO1, heme oxygenase-1 and superoxide dismutase, and as suppressing NF-kB signalling and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6.[14] Grokipedia also describes histone deacetylase inhibition.[14] In the 2007 skin work, the authors describe the protection as acting through phase 2 enzymes rather than by blocking UV light, which is why a lead author said the extract is not simply a sunscreen.[4][5]

A 2024 review of hormesis, the idea that low doses of mild stressors trigger protective responses, lists sulforaphane among dietary supplements examined for lifespan extension in model organisms, and a 2021 study reported that sulforaphane extended lifespan and healthspan in the worm C. elegans through insulin/IGF-1 signalling.[17][18] These are laboratory findings in animals, not skin outcomes in people.

subs.h: Topical sprout extract and UV redness
paras: The most cited skin study is Talalay and colleagues' paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (30 October 2007). The team found that extracts from three-day-old broccoli sprouts activated phase 2 enzymes in mouse and human skin, reduced inflammation and swelling in mice, and lessened redness from narrow-band UV in humans. In six adults, redness fell by an average of 37.7 percent, with a range from 8.37 to 78.1 percent (P = 0.025).[4]

News coverage from the time reported that the extract still protected when applied three days before UV exposure, that responses varied from 8 to 78 percent between volunteers, and that conventional sunscreens were described as ineffective in these experiments, while the lead author, Talalay, said that 'the protection lasts for several days'.[5] The study was small, funded by the NIH and charitable groups, and used a topical extract rather than a food or capsule.[4][5]

No published trial has measured skin appearance, wrinkles or complexion after eating sprouts or taking capsules. Proponents extend the topical finding to oral intake on the grounds that the same cellular pathway is engaged, while the trials of oral products examine other outcomes.[2][9][10]

A 2025 Nature Microbiology randomized, double-blind trial gave broccoli sprout extract (n = 35) or placebo (n = 39) daily for 12 weeks in people with prediabetes. The primary target, a 0.3 mmol/l fasting glucose reduction versus placebo, was not met; the overall difference was 0.2 mmol/l, with a stronger response in a subgroup with mild obesity, low insulin resistance and reduced insulin secretion. Gastrointestinal side effects but no severe adverse events were reported.[9] A 2024 randomized trial examined sulforaphane for insulin resistance through gut-microbe signalling.[19]

In children with autism spectrum disorder, a randomized controlled trial and metabolite study was published in Molecular Autism in 2021, and a 2022 network meta-analysis of pharmacological and supplement treatments for autism also covers the field.[10][20] A 2025 randomized trial studied sulforaphane added to methylphenidate for ADHD in 70 children aged 6 to 11, and a 2021 randomized trial studied an adjunctive sulforaphane nutraceutical in schizophrenia.[11][12] A 2025 randomized phase II trial studied sulforaphane in former smokers at high risk for lung cancer.[13]

The Linus Pauling Institute summarises further small human studies: increased antioxidant enzymes in the airway of people given sprout homogenate, no induction of Nrf2-pathway markers in a four-week COPD trial, reduced histone deacetylase activity in blood cells after about 68 g of sprouts, and mixed results in H. pylori, prostate and breast tissue studies.[3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: On T Nation, sulforaphane appears mainly in threads on hormone balance and supplements. Posters list it alongside DIM and calcium D-glucarate in stacks they say lower estrogen, with one reporting no noticeable effect from a combination and another describing 'great results' with such a stack.[6][21] Another thread cites sulforaphane as a food-based histone deacetylase inhibitor said to raise follistatin, a myostatin-related protein, in a discussion of muscle growth.[7] A thread on androgen receptors after finasteride speculates about using sulforaphane or rosemary to reduce receptor numbers, which is the poster's theory rather than a documented use.[22]

Some bodybuilders mention it simply as a reason to keep broccoli in the diet instead of replacing vegetables with a processed product.[23] Others discuss whether organic broccoli carries less sulforaphane than conventional.[24]
A Hacker News submission, titled as describing sulforaphane as a tool to fight cancer, ageing and inflammatory issues, reflects the wider longevity-minded interest.[25]

The Linus Pauling Institute states that no serious adverse effects of isothiocyanates in humans have been reported, and notes that very high doses of other isothiocyanates promoted bladder cancer in rats after carcinogen exposure, that there are no data on purified isothiocyanates or high-dose supplements in pregnancy or lactation, and that isothiocyanates may inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes.[3] The prediabetes trial reported gastrointestinal side effects.[9] Sulforaphane is sold as a food compound and dietary supplement, and Wikipedia states there is no good clinical evidence of benefit from sulforaphane-rich vegetables or supplements for disease prevention.[1]

Related approaches include eating other cruciferous vegetables, taking DIM or indole-3-carbinol products from crucifers, using other plant antioxidants such as green tea extract in diet or skincare, and daily sunscreen for UV protection. Reviews of sulfoxides in medicine place sulforaphane among natural sulfoxide compounds of pharmaceutical interest.

timeline.event: Sulforaphane is isolated and characterised from broccoli by Paul Talalay and colleagues at Johns Hopkins, according to Grokipedia.[14]
Talalay and colleagues publish in PNAS that topical broccoli sprout extract reduced UV-induced redness in six volunteers by an average of 37.7 percent.[4][5]
Linus Pauling Institute isothiocyanate summary last updated, reviewing human studies of sprouts and sulforaphane.[3]
Journal of Medicinal Food review summarises sulforaphane properties for cancer, cardiovascular risk, autism and osteoporosis.[2]
Randomized controlled trial in children with autism spectrum disorder; schizophrenia adjunct trial; C. elegans lifespan study.[10][12][17]
Network meta-analysis of autism treatments includes dietary supplements.[20]
Nature Microbiology prediabetes trial of broccoli sprout extract; ADHD and lung-cancer prevention trials published.[9][11][13]
